blocks.title: Positivity and square roots
blocks.tex: Throughout this section, $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner product space over $\R$ or $\C$. Spectral theory lets us compare positive operators with nonnegative real numbers and construct their distinguished square roots.

blocks.title: Positive operators
blocks.tex: An operator $T\in\Lin(V)$ is positive if it is self-adjoint and $\ip{Tv}{v}\ge0$ for every $v\in V$. This inequality requires the inner-product value to be real. The term positive includes the zero operator; another name is positive semidefinite.

blocks.title: Positivity from quadratic values over the complex field
blocks.tex: Over $\C$, the condition $\ip{Tv}{v}\ge0$ for every $v$ already implies that $T$ is positive.
blocks.proof: All the stated quadratic values are real, so the complex quadratic-value criterion makes $T$ self-adjoint. Together with the assumed nonnegativity, this is exactly the definition of positivity.
hints: Use the real-quadratic-value criterion for self-adjointness.

blocks.title: A positive coordinate operator
blocks.tex: On $\F^2$ with the standard inner product, $T(x,y)=(2x-y,-x+y)$ is positive.
blocks.proof:
The coordinate formula defines a linear operator. Its standard matrix is real symmetric, hence equals its conjugate transpose. Because the standard basis is orthonormal, this proves self-adjointness. Direct expansion gives
\[\ip{T(x,y)}{(x,y)}=2|x|^2-x\overline y-y\overline x+|y|^2=|x-y|^2+|x|^2\ge0.\]
The last equality follows by multiplying $(x-y)(\overline x-\overline y)$. Thus both conditions for positivity hold.
hints: Check self-adjointness and express the quadratic value as a sum of squared moduli.

blocks.title: Orthogonal projections are positive
blocks.tex: For any subspace $U\subseteq V$, the orthogonal projection $P_U$ is positive.
blocks.proof:
Write $v=P_Uv+v_\perp$ and $w=P_Uw+w_\perp$, with the remainder vectors in $U^\perp$. Orthogonality gives
\[\ip{P_Uv}{w}=\ip{P_Uv}{P_Uw}=\ip{v}{P_Uw}.\]
The inner-product test therefore makes $P_U$ self-adjoint. Taking $w=v$ gives $\ip{P_Uv}{v}=\|P_Uv\|^2\ge0$, so it is positive. The decomposition theorem applies because $U$ is finite-dimensional as a subspace of $V$, including $U=\{0\}$.
hints: Decompose both inputs into their $U$ and $U^\perp$ components.

blocks.title: Positive quadratics in a self-adjoint operator
blocks.tex: If $T$ is self-adjoint and $b,c\in\R$ satisfy $b^2<4c$, then $T^2+bT+cI$ is positive. Its quadratic value is strictly positive at every nonzero vector.
blocks.proof:
The adjoint rules show that $T^2+bT+cI$ is self-adjoint, because $T^*=T$ and the coefficients are real. Put $A=T+(b/2)I$, which is also self-adjoint. Completing the square gives
\[T^2+bT+cI=A^2+(c-b^2/4)I.\]
For any $v$, self-adjointness of $A$ gives $\ip{A^2v}{v}=\ip{Av}{Av}=\|Av\|^2$. Thus the quadratic value of the displayed operator is $\|Av\|^2+(c-b^2/4)\|v\|^2$. Both terms are nonnegative, and for $v\ne0$ the second is positive because $c-b^2/4>0$. This proves both conclusions.
hints: Complete the square in the operator and move one self-adjoint factor across the inner product.

blocks.title: Square roots of an operator
blocks.tex: A square root of $T\in\Lin(V)$ is an operator $R\in\Lin(V)$ with $R^2=T$. This definition alone imposes no positivity or self-adjointness condition.

blocks.title: A square root supplied by a coordinate shift
blocks.tex: The operator $R(x,y,z)=(y,z,0)$ is a square root of $T(x,y,z)=(z,0,0)$ on $\F^3$.
blocks.proof: Both formulas are linear by the coordinate characterization. Applying $R$ twice gives $R^2(x,y,z)=R(y,z,0)=(z,0,0)=T(x,y,z)$ for every input. Therefore $R^2=T$, which is the square-root condition.

blocks.title: Equivalent descriptions of a positive operator
blocks.tex:
For $T\in\Lin(V)$ the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $T$ is positive.
\item $T$ is self-adjoint and all its eigenvalues are nonnegative.
\item Some orthonormal basis gives a diagonal matrix for $T$ with nonnegative diagonal entries.
\item $T$ has a positive square root.
\item $T$ has a self-adjoint square root.
\item $T=R^*R$ for some $R\in\Lin(V)$.
\end{enumerate}
blocks.proof:
We prove a cycle of implications. Suppose first $T$ is positive. It is self-adjoint by definition. For an eigenvector $v$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$, $0\le\ip{Tv}{v}=\lambda\|v\|^2$, and $\|v\|^2>0$. Thus $\lambda$ is nonnegative, proving the second condition.
A self-adjoint operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis: use the real spectral theorem over $\R$, and self-adjointness implies normality so the complex spectral theorem applies over $\C$. Under the second condition its eigenvalues are nonnegative, so this basis gives the third condition.
Assume the third condition, with $Te_j=\lambda_je_j$ and $\lambda_j\ge0$. Prescribe $Re_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}e_j$ on this basis. The basis prescription theorem gives a linear operator. Its matrix is real diagonal in an orthonormal basis, so $R$ is self-adjoint. If $v=\sum_ja_je_j$, expansion yields $\ip{Rv}{v}=\sum_j\sqrt{\lambda_j}|a_j|^2\ge0$. Hence $R$ is positive. Furthermore $R^2e_j=\lambda_je_j=Te_j$ on every basis vector, so $R^2=T$. This proves the fourth condition.
Every positive operator is self-adjoint, so the fourth implies the fifth. If $R$ is a self-adjoint square root, then $T=R^2=R^*R$, proving the sixth. Finally suppose $T=R^*R$. The adjoint rules give $T^*=(R^*R)^*=R^*(R^*)^*=R^*R=T$. The adjoint identity gives $\ip{Tv}{v}=\ip{R^*Rv}{v}=\ip{Rv}{Rv}=\|Rv\|^2\ge0$, proving positivity and completing the cycle. If $V=\{0\}$, all bases and diagonal lists used here are empty and all operators coincide with zero, so every construction and implication still applies.
hints: Use the spectral theorem to pass from eigenvalue information to an orthonormal diagonal matrix.
Take nonnegative scalar square roots on an eigenbasis.
For the last implication, calculate the quadratic value of $R^*R$.

blocks.title: Uniqueness of the positive square root
blocks.tex: Every positive operator has exactly one positive square root. If $Tv=\lambda v$, that square root satisfies $Rv=\sqrt\lambda v$ for every such eigenvector.
blocks.proof:
Existence is one of the equivalent positivity conditions. Let $R$ be any positive square root, and let $v\ne0$ satisfy $Tv=\lambda v$. Positivity gives $\lambda\ge0$. The characterization applied to $R$ supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ with $Re_j=\mu_je_j$ and $\mu_j\ge0$. Write $v=\sum_ja_je_j$. The identity $R^2v=Tv=\lambda v$ and basis independence imply $a_j(\mu_j^2-\lambda)=0$ for every $j$. If $a_j\ne0$, then $\mu_j^2=\lambda$, and nonnegativity makes $\mu_j=\sqrt\lambda$. Therefore
\[Rv=\sum_ja_j\mu_je_j=\sqrt\lambda\sum_ja_je_j=\sqrt\lambda v.\]
This proves the stated action on every eigenvector of $T$, regardless of which positive square root was chosen. Since $T$ has an eigenvector basis by the positivity characterization, any two positive square roots agree on a basis and are equal. On the zero space there is only one operator, which is its own positive square root, so uniqueness holds there as well.
hints: Expand an eigenvector of $T$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis of a proposed positive square root.
Nonnegative scalar square roots are unique.

blocks.title: The identity can have infinitely many square roots
blocks.tex: If $\dim V\ge2$, the identity operator has infinitely many square roots, although its unique positive square root is itself.
blocks.proof: Choose a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ with $n\ge2$. For each real $t$ prescribe $R_tv_1=v_1$, $R_tv_2=tv_1-v_2$, and $R_tv_j=v_j$ for $j\ge3$. These values define a linear operator. Applying it twice gives $R_t^2v_1=v_1$, $R_t^2v_2=tv_1-(tv_1-v_2)=v_2$, and $R_t^2v_j=v_j$ at all remaining indices. Thus $R_t^2=I$. Distinct $t$ give different values on $v_2$, hence different operators, and there are infinitely many real choices. The identity is self-adjoint and has quadratic values $\|v\|^2\ge0$, so it is positive and is its own square root. The positive-square-root uniqueness theorem therefore singles out $I$ among all these square roots.
hints: Construct an involution on two basis vectors with a freely chosen scalar.

blocks.title: The positive square root notation
blocks.tex: For a positive operator $T$, write $\sqrt T$ for its unique positive square root.

blocks.title: Two explicit positive square roots
blocks.tex:
On $\R^2$ let $S(x,y)=(x,2y)$ and $T(x,y)=(x+y,x+y)$. Both are positive, and
\[\sqrt S(x,y)=(x,\sqrt2y),\qquad\sqrt T(x,y)=\frac1{\sqrt2}(x+y,x+y).\]
blocks.proof: Both standard matrices are real symmetric, hence the operators are self-adjoint. Their quadratic values are $x^2+2y^2$ and $(x+y)^2$, respectively, which are nonnegative. Thus both are positive. The proposed square root of $S$ is real diagonal, hence self-adjoint, with nonnegative quadratic value $x^2+\sqrt2y^2$. Its square is $S$ by direct substitution. For the second formula put $R=T/\sqrt2$. Its matrix is real symmetric and its quadratic value is $(x+y)^2/\sqrt2\ge0$, so it is positive. Direct composition gives $T^2(x,y)=2(x+y,x+y)=2T(x,y)$, hence $R^2=T$. Uniqueness of positive square roots identifies both displayed operators as the designated square roots.
hints: Check both the square and positivity of each proposed answer.

blocks.title: A zero quadratic value detects the kernel of a positive operator
blocks.tex:
For a positive operator $T$ and any $v$,
\[\ip{Tv}{v}=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Tv=0.\]
blocks.proof:
Write $R=\sqrt T$, so $R^*=R$ and $R^2=T$. Then
\[\ip{Tv}{v}=\ip{R^2v}{v}=\ip{Rv}{Rv}=\|Rv\|^2.\]
If this is zero, norm definiteness gives $Rv=0$, hence $Tv=R(Rv)=R0=0$ by linearity. Conversely if $Tv=0$, its inner product with $v$ is zero by the zero inner-product identity. This proves both directions, including the zero vector.
hints: Express the quadratic value as a squared norm involving the positive square root.

cards.front: What are the two requirements for positivity?
How do eigenvalues characterize positivity for a self-adjoint operator?
Which square root of a positive operator is unique?
cards.back: Its positive square root; arbitrary square roots need not be unique.

cards.front: How does $\sqrt T$ act on an eigenvector of positive $T$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$?
cards.back: It multiplies the vector by the nonnegative scalar $\sqrt\lambda$.
